clinicalPearls: Classic triad of epileptic (infantile) spasms, hypsarrhythmia on EEG, and developmental arrest or regression.
Onset is typically between 3 and 12 months, peaking around 4 to 7 months.
Spasms occur in clusters, often on awakening, with brief symmetrical flexion or extension of trunk and limbs.
Aetiology is diverse: structural (tuberous sclerosis, cortical malformation, hypoxic-ischaemic injury), genetic or metabolic, or unknown.
Hypsarrhythmia is a chaotic, high-amplitude, disorganised interictal pattern; modified or fragmented variants occur.
First-line treatments are hormonal therapy (adrenocorticotrophic hormone or corticosteroids) and vigabatrin, the latter being especially effective in tuberous sclerosis.
Prompt recognition and treatment improve developmental outcome, reflecting a treatment-lag effect.
The condition may evolve into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome or other epilepsies.
reference.pathophysiology: West syndrome reflects age-specific hyperexcitability of the developing brain. Diverse structural, genetic and metabolic insults converge on dysregulated cortical, subcortical and brainstem networks during a critical developmental window; proposed contributors include abnormal corticotrophin-releasing hormone signalling and an imbalance of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission. The result is the characteristic clustered spasms and disorganised hypsarrhythmic EEG, with disruption of normal synaptic maturation contributing to developmental regression.
additionalDifferentials: Benign non-epileptic infantile spasms and benign myoclonus of infancy
Early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (Ohtahara)
Startle responses and benign sleep myoclonus
additionalInvestigations: Prolonged or video EEG including sleep to confirm hypsarrhythmia and capture spasms
MRI brain to identify a structural cause
Metabolic screen including consideration of pyridoxine-dependent and biotinidase disorders
Genetic testing (chromosomal microarray, gene panels or exome)
Skin examination and imaging for tuberous sclerosis
Therapeutic trial of pyridoxine where indicated
redFlags: Clusters of spasms, especially on waking
Focal neurological signs suggesting a structural lesion
Features of raised intracranial pressure or an underlying metabolic crisis
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on aetiology and treatment lag; cryptogenic cases treated promptly may do well, whereas symptomatic cases often have persistent epilepsy and intellectual disability, and many evolve into other epilepsy syndromes.
pitfalls: Mistaking spasms for colic, reflux or startle and delaying diagnosis.
Not obtaining a sleep EEG and thereby missing hypsarrhythmia.
Prolonging the treatment lag by delaying therapy.
Overlooking tuberous sclerosis, which changes drug choice.
Failing to investigate for treatable metabolic causes.
references: ILAE position papers on classification of the epilepsies and epileptic spasms
Panayiotopoulos CP. A Clinical Guide to Epileptic Syndromes and their Treatment
management: Start first-line hormonal therapy with adrenocorticotrophic hormone or oral corticosteroids such as prednisolone to suppress the spasms
Use vigabatrin as an alternative first-line agent, and preferentially where tuberous sclerosis is the underlying cause
Treat promptly to minimise the treatment lag, as early control improves developmental outcome
Identify and address the underlying aetiology, including a trial of pyridoxine for pyridoxine-dependent seizures and targeted management of metabolic or structural causes
Repeat EEG to confirm resolution of hypsarrhythmia and cessation of spasms as the treatment endpoint
Arrange long-term developmental surveillance and support, anticipating possible evolution to other epilepsy syndromes
Refer to paediatric neurology, and offer genetic counselling where a genetic cause is identified
